If you are looking for a solution to this problem, besides the very relevant solutions suggested to you in the comment section, you can use the library to compute power for a range of prespecified sample sizes, and find which ones meet your criteria (instead of trying to find the sample size for a specified power). From that, you can draw a power curve (which may be more informative than just a point sample size and power), and also determine the smallest sample size that will give you a power of at least 0.95. It can be computationally intensive to calculate power over a very large range of sample sizes, so in some cases you might want to use a trial-and-error approach, and test a couple of plausible sample sizes first before searching over a range of values. Here is an example in R, where we compute power for a range of sample sizes between 480,000 and 490,000, and store the resulting power at each iteration:. pw = pwr.2p.test(h=h, sig.level=alpha, n=sample.size)$power. Then we can draw a power curve to get a better idea of the situation, and see easily how reducing or increasing the sample size would impact power:. `plot(sample.sizes, powers, type = "l", ylab = "power", xlab = "sample size", main = "Power curve for. A power curve, with sample size on the horizontal axis, and power on the vertical axis. A power curve, with sample size on the horizontal axis, and power on the vertical axis. It should be quite easy to find what is the smallest sample size that gives a power of a least 0.95:. `n = min(sample.sizes[powers >= 0.95]). You can check which actual power you get with this sample size:. `pwr.2p.test(h=h, sig.level=alpha, n=n)$power #0.9500003`. Note that in some circumstances, searching the smallest sample size without looking at the details of the power curve can leave you unaware of a few bad surprises, in particular if you have very strict requirements relative to power. ## Your Answer. results.title: Sample size calculations for stepped wedge and cluster randomised trials: a unified approach
results.content: To clarify and illustrate sample size calculations for the cross-sectional stepped wedge cluster randomized trial (SW-CRT) and to present a simple approach for comparing the efficiencies of competing designs within a unified framework. **Keywords:** Stepped wedge, Cluster randomized trial, Power, Sample size, Efficiency, Study design. Our specific objectives are to (1) illustrate, by example, how to implement design effects in the SW-CRT to ensure correct sample size calculations under a variety of scenarios; (2) demonstrate that the SW-CRT does not always require a smaller total sample size or smaller number of clusters than the parallel CRT; and (3) provide novel sample size methodology to allow designers to determine required cluster size in the SW-CRT, as current published design effects allow computation of the number of clusters, but not number of subjects per cluster. For example, under the SW-CRT design with _t_ steps, the total study sample size is km(_t_+1), that is, the number of clusters _k_ multiplied by the number of time points _t_+1 and the number of observations made in each cluster per time point _m_. Following on from this work, a design effect for stepped wedge studies has been derived, which allows determination of number of clusters needed for a given sample size per cluster per period (_m_) and number of steps (_t_) . For the SW-CRT design, results are presented for either two or five steps, implying cluster sizes per period of either m=10 or 50. For a planned clustered design, we consider both small (0.01), moderate (0.1), and large (0.25) anticipated ICCs and compare the power achievable or sample size required (both number of clusters and cluster size) among the three design choices under consideration here (the parallel CRT, the CRT-BA, and the SW-CRT). Example: design effects (DEs), total required study sizes (_N_), and number of clusters (_k_) required under each design given fixed total cluster sizes _M_ and ICC (_ρ_). Example: required total sample sizes per cluster (_M_) and total study size (_N_) under each design given fixed number of clusters _k_ and ICC (_ρ_). Stepped wedge designs could reduce the required sample size in cluster randomized trials.

Title: How to calculate statistical power for your meta-analysis | by Dan Quintana | TDS Archive | Medium
# How to calculate statistical power for your meta-analysis. Meta-analysis is a popular approach to synthesize a body of research that addresses a specific research question. However, statistical power is rarely considered when planning or interpreting a meta-analysis. This is probably due to the fact that there is no accessible software or R script to calculate meta-analytic power, like G\*Power or the “pwr” R package, which are great options for calculating statistical power for primary research. Thanks to formulas available from this paper, I wrote my own script to calculate power for a random-effects meta-analysis. Just enter your anticipated summary effect size, average number of participants per group, total number of effect sizes, and study heterogeneity in the following script. Here’s a look at statistical power for a series of heterogeneity levels, summary effect sizes, group sample sizes, and total number of included sample sizes. Effect sizes of d = 0.2, d = 0.5, and d = 0.8 are considered small, medium, and large effect sizes. It’s interesting that under most circumstances, meta-analyses are sufficiently powered to detect large summary effect sizes (bottom row). However, they struggle to have sufficient power to detect small effects in most circumstances (top row). The power to detect medium effects (middle row) is a mixed bag, and seems to be largely dependent on study heterogeneity. **UPDATE:** Thank you to Jakob Tiebel, who has put together an Excel calculator to calculate statistical power for your meta-analysis using the same formulas. Want a step-by-step guide to performing your own correlational meta-analysis? Here’s our episode on meta-analysis. results.title: Effect sizes and intra-cluster correlation coefficients measured from the Green Dot High School study for guiding sample size calculations when designing future violence prevention cluster randomized trials in school settings - PMC
results.content: To help guide future study planning, we provide information on anticipated effect sizes and intra-cluster correlation coefficients (ICCs), as well as school sizes, for dating violence (DV) and interpersonal violence outcomes based on data from a cRCT which evaluated the bystander-based violence intervention *‘Green Dot’*. Besides the desired significance level, power, and effect size, numerical information is needed on school sizes (number of subjects from whom data are collected) and the intra-cluster correlation coefficient (ICC) [9], which quantifies the degree of clustering. Utilizing data from the Green Dot High School (GDHS) study, we provide information on observed school sizes, effect sizes, and ICC values specific to victimization and perpetration outcomes related to sexual and dating violence in teens. In order to calculate the required number of clusters to design a cRCT to assess the efficacy of the intervention versus control, information on desired level of significance (α), type II error rate (β=1−power), the standard deviation of the outcome variable, the cluster size ( m‾; the average high school size), the ICC, and the effect size are needed.
